newsitem.title: USA: Most Georgia school tax referendums approved.
newsitem.headline: Most Georgia school tax referendums approved.

text.p: Georgia voters overwhelmingly approved local sales tax increases to pay for a flurry of school construction and retire oustanding debt, education and elections officials said Wednesday.
Of 69 school districts voting Tuesday, only four rejected the increases, according to a preliminary check with school officials, elections supervisors and local newspapers.

"We are delighted it was that successful," said Dr. Don Rooks, director of government operations for the Georgia School Boards Association. "Systems vary and the needs vary and the perception of how to meet those needs varies. That's the beauty of having a county-by-county sales tax."
Georgia voters approved a constitutional amendment in November allowing districts to levy the one-cent tax increase for up to five years for capital projects and early debt retirement.
Sixty-nine of the state's 180 school districts rushed to put the proposals on the ballot on Tuesday, the earliest the elections could be held.

Four failed. Voters in Atkinson County rejected the tax hike with 57 percent of voters against, Chattooga County with 56 percent against, Hart County with 58 percent against and Toombs County with 68 percent against.
But the remaining 65 referendums were aprpoved by margins ranging from 52 percent in Coweta County to 97 percent in Jasper County.
In Fulton County, the referendum passed with 62 percent of the vote, even though Fulton voters defeated the November ballot amendment authorizing it.

"We were very pleased that since November, we were able to get the information out and get people out and vote. I think it was a tremendous effort from our parents, our business partners, our community and our staff," said Fulton schools spokeswoman Mitzi Edge.

Fulton plans to retire $61 million of bonds early but will use most of the anticipated $490 million in new revenues for new construction. Rooks predicted most districts would follow a similar pattern.
"I would guess that in most of them, there's some retirement of bonds and a great deal of renovation and some construction," he said.
Several other school systems tentatively plan similar referendums in June.
"I think they will be encouraged by the vote," Rooks said.

Previously, most Georgia school construction was funded with 30-year bonds backed by property taxes. In many places, the new sales tax revenue will be an addition rather than a replacement for property taxes.

"I think it's safe to say the property tax has been quite burdensome thus far," Rooks said. "I think most people would like to see a property tax cut, but whether a given individual system can cut it or merely not raise it more to meet growing needs will vary."
